newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU sides with U.S. in film trade row with Japan.
newsitem.headline: EU sides with U.S. in film trade row with Japan.

text.p: The European Union, lining up with the United States in a major dispute, told a World Trade Organisation (WTO) panel on Friday it saw the Japanese photofilm market as skewed to favour domestic producers.
The EU view was presented to the three-man panel during its first oral hearings on the U.S. and Japanese positions in the multi-billion dollar row, widely known as the "Kodak-Fuji" case.

EU envoys told the panel they saw the heart of the case as "lack of access to the main distribution channels" in Japan for foreign film and photopaper which resulted from Japanese government measures, EU officials said.

But they also said some aspects of the dispute related to the trade effects of anti-competitive practices, underlining what Brussels argues is a need for WTO members to pursue the issue of the link between trade and competition policy.
The EU has not launched a case of its own against Tokyo, but has adopted an "interested third party" stance.

Like the United States, which launched two cases against Japan on the issue in June last year, Brussels says that its complaint focuses on practices that run against WTO rules or nullify open trade accords, and insists it is not acting on behalf of individual companies.

But the EU move is clearly linked to problems of the main European photofilm producer, Germany's Agfa-Gevaert, in Japan's domestic market which industry officials say are similar to those encountered by the U.S. Eastman Kodak.
Agfa-Gevaert Japan Ltd, a Bayer group company, has a some five per cent of photofilm and paper sales.

Both the United States and the EU are now arguing that the Japanese government has encouraged close links between retailers and distributors effectively ensuring that Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd products dominate shop shelves in Japan.

Kodak, which holds 70 percent of the U.S. domestic market but only nine per cent in Japan, says that for two decades it has lost up to $5.6 billion annually in potential sales because of unfair Japanese market practices.

Fuji, which holds 67 per cent of its home market, says that it faces distribution barriers in the United States, where it holds about 12 per cent. Fuji representatives in Europe argue the Japanese company encounters similar problems in the EU.
Japan rejects the U.S. and EU charges of market rigging, saying its market is open and arguing that foreign companies' success depends on the sales effort they apply.

The panel, whose members were appointed in December last year, would normally be expected to deliver its findings by the middle of June, but diplomats say the complicated nature of case could cause a delay of several weeks or even months.

Among problems faced by the panel, trade envoys say, is obtaining neutral translation of volumes of Japanese government regulations and instructions which U.S. officials say ensure domestic products are favoured.
